# 012 · Deleting the hold sweeper, proved safe for every interleaving

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: all invariants hold in 3,604 states** | no-false-positive | none | cleanup, behaviour change not intended | [`HoldService#releaseExpiredHolds`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/app/HoldService.java) | [D1: Protocol model checking](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/spec/README.md) |

> The scheduled job that releases expired holds looks load-bearing: without it, seats of expired holds stay marked HELD. A developer deletes it anyway, and the model checker confirms that every safety invariant still holds in every reachable state, because the rest of the system already treats an expired hold as free.

## The change

Remove `HoldService.releaseExpiredHolds`, its schedule, and its setting. The job's own comment claims that correctness does not depend on it; the developer takes the claim at its word and removes the moving part, and removes the matching `Sweep` action from the TLA+ model.

**Before** ([`HoldService.java`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/app/HoldService.java), line 9):

```java
import net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.domain.HoldPolicy;
import net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.store.HoldDocument;
import net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.store.TicketingStore;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

/**
    // ...
@Service
public class HoldService {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(HoldService.class);

    private final TicketingStore store;
    private final Transactions transactions;
    private final HoldPolicy policy;
    // ...
    public HoldDocument get(String holdId) {
        return store.hold(holdId).orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException("no hold " + holdId));
    }

    /**
     * Releases expired holds. Correctness does not depend on this: a new hold already treats an expired seat as free.
     * The sweep keeps the stored status honest for readers and for the order flow.
     */
    @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${boxoffice.hold.sweep-interval:1s}")
    public void releaseExpiredHolds() {
        long released = store.releaseExpired(clock.instant());
        if (released > 0) {
            log.info("Released {} seats whose hold expired", released);
        }
    }
}
```

**After:**


## What the verifier found

Every invariant holds in every reachable state of the model: 3,604 distinct states, which is every interleaving of the customers, the two services, Kafka and the clock within the model's bounds (Customers = {alice, bob}, Seats = {s1}, MaxTime = 3, HoldTtl = 1).

The order state machine inside the model is generated from the behavioural contract of the patched code, so the model checks the decisions the services really make.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`:ticketing-service:test`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

None, if the comment is right. The risk the example addresses is the other one: code that nobody dares delete because nobody can say what it protects. A model that covers every interleaving can say it. Here it says that no double sale, no stranded money and no disagreement between the services becomes reachable when the sweeper is gone, because hold expiry is checked at every point that matters, by comparing timestamps rather than by trusting a stored status.

## Why the verdict is right

With the `Sweep` action removed, TLC explores every reachable state of the smaller system and finds no violation of any invariant. The result is specific to the safety properties the model states; it says nothing about the display of availability or about how long a seat stays marked HELD, which are the sweeper's actual job. Deleting it is safe, and also makes the seat list lie to readers until the next hold, which is a product decision rather than a correctness one.

## What to do

Safe to merge as far as correctness goes. Keep the sweeper if the seat list is read directly by anything that does not compare expiry times.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: TLC 2.19 explored 3,604 distinct states to depth 26 in 00 s, for the model Customers = {alice, bob}, Seats = {s1}, MaxTime = 3, HoldTtl = 1.
